summary: timeweave 1.4.0 fetches attacker-controlled manifest and executes downloaded payloads on Windows via WinExec
details: The package advertises itself as a timezone data cache but ships a hidden dropper. Calling the public API functions detect_timezone() or convert_timezone() invokes _ensure_cache, which starts a daemon thread named 'curls-autoupdate' that runs updater._sync_database. The sync path fetches a JSON manifest from https://timezone.api.globaltimedata.com/latest/db.json (a host unrelated to the declared github.com/vxmpingz publisher), parses extensions.assets/resources entries, downloads each url to a /tmp/firebeta_* workspace, and on Windows executes each staged file via ctypes.windll.kernel32.WinExec. The manifest server controls both the URLs downloaded and the commands passed to WinExec, giving that server arbitrary code execution on Windows installers. The README claims 'Fetch + SHA-256 verify + cache' and a _fetch_checksum helper exists, but the sync path never calls it — _check_locked writes the fetched bytes and records its own local digest without comparing any published checksum, and the manifest's integrity field is optional. Errors in the extension-execution branch are silently swallowed, so no failure is surfaced to the caller.

cwes.description: The product contains code that appears to be malicious in nature.
cwes.name: Embedded Malicious Code
